title: Robustness analysis of watermarking techniques for LLM-generated code
authors: Dingyi Cao; Siyuan Liu; Jing Zhang; Yuan Xiang
abstract: The widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) for code generation raises critical concerns regarding authorship attribution and accountability, motivating the development of watermarking techniques to trace model outputs, though the practical utility of these approaches depends on their robustness against real-world adversarial conditions, including code transformations and model adaptation. The paper systematically evaluates two state-of-the-art watermarking paradigms: SWEET, which embeds token-level statistical biases, and CodeMark, which leverages semantic-preserving transformations at the statement level. The researchers designed experiments under two adversarial settings: (i) spoofing attacks and (ii) watermark-removal attacks; empirical results reveal that the robustness of different watermarking schemes differs under varying attack scenarios, but all lack resistance in adversarial environments.
inclusion_reason: Code-watermarking robustness study. Directly code-watermarking-specific: it stress-tests two methods already in our corpus (SWEET, CodeMark/Sun) under spoofing and removal attacks, giving independent robustness evidence we can cite alongside their own self-reported results.

title: Disappearing ink: Obfuscation breaks n-gram code watermarks in theory and practice
authors: Gehao Zhang; Eugene Bagdasarian; Juan Zhai; et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code generation, making reliable identification of machine-generated code important for attribution, tracking, and misuse detection. Existing code watermarking methods are dominated by N-gram-based schemes, yet their robustness has mostly been evaluated only against simple edits or optimizations. We argue that this significantly overstates security, because software engineering already provides stronger semantics-preserving transformations in the form of code obfuscation. We study N-gram-based code watermarking under obfuscation. We formally model semantics-preserving transformations as a Markov random walk and prove that, under an intuitive and experimentally supported assumption called distribution consistency, obfuscation can nullify the robustness of N-gram-based watermarks. If the original detector has a false positive rate fpr, then after obfuscation, its failure rate on watermarked code approaches 1 - fpr. We validate this theory on three state-of-the-art watermarking schemes, two LLMs, two programming languages, four benchmarks, and four obfuscators. Across all settings, detectors collapse to near-random performance on obfuscated code (AUROC tightly around 0.5), and for each language, at least one attack leaves all post-obfuscation AUROC scores below 0.6. These results jointly show that current N-gram-based code watermarks are not robust to realistic obfuscation attacks and motivate more semantics-aware alternatives.
inclusion_reason: Code-watermarking robustness study. Entirely code-watermarking-specific: a formal + empirical robustness analysis of the exact token-biasing paradigm (WLLM/SWEET-style) that dominates our included corpus (9 of 20 methods), directly relevant to the robustness dimension of RQ3.

title: Can we trust the source? A systematic review of watermarking and attribution for AI-generated code
authors: Istiaq Ahmed Fahad; Mridha Md. Nafis Fuad
abstract: Context: Large Language Models (LLMs) are now widely used in software engineering, especially for code generation tasks. While this has improved developer productivity, it has also raised several concerns. Issues related to intellectual property (IP), academic integrity, and software supply chain security are becoming more common. At the same time, AI-generated code is increasingly hard to distinguish from human-written code. Because of this, identifying the origin of source code has become an important and challenging problem. Objectives: This study aims to systematically analyze and compare existing techniques for tracing the provenance of AI-generated source code, with a focus on two dominant paradigms: active provenance mechanisms (code watermarking) and passive provenance mechanisms (authorship attribution). The goal is to assess their effectiveness, robustness, and practical suitability within real-world software engineering workflows. Method: We performed a Systematic Literature Review following the PRISMA guidelines. The review covers studies published from 2020 to 2025. A quality assessment rubric was designed with a focus on code executability and security relevance. Studies that did not validate functional correctness or lacked sufficient experimental detail were excluded. After filtering, 31 primary studies were selected for detailed analysis. Results: The review reveals a clear trade-off between deployability and reliability. Passive attribution techniques are non-intrusive and easy to deploy, but degrade significantly under common code transformations such as refactoring or variable renaming. Active watermarking methods provide stronger verifiability and ownership guarantees while generally preserving functionality and readability. However, many token-level schemes remain fragile under semantic-preserving transformations. Syntax-aware and semantic-level approaches demonstrate improved robustness but incur higher computational costs. Conclusion: Overall, existing provenance techniques are largely non-intrusive and suitable for clean environments. Current research tends to favor accuracy and invisibility over long-term robustness. Future work should focus more on semantic-level resilience and adopt shared adversarial benchmarks to better reflect real-world threats.
inclusion_reason: Closest comparable systematic review (active + passive scope). Fully code-watermarking-specific and the single closest comparable work: an independent PRISMA review of 31 code-provenance studies (both watermarking and attribution). Its 31-study list is the most valuable cross-check for corpus completeness, but its full text/reference list is paywalled (SSRN and ResearchGate both blocked access attempts) — worth revisiting with institutional access.

title: AI Generated Code Plagiarism Detection in Computer Science Courses: A Literature Mapping
authors: Archer Simmons; Maristela Holanda; Christiana Chamon; Dilma Da Silva
abstract: Addresses how integrity in the detection of plagiarism in students' source code in university programming courses is an important research topic, particularly in introductory courses like CS1. Notes that with the latest developments in Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot, methods of plagiarism have evolved, and that detection methods may not be capable of accurately differentiating between human- and AI-generated code. Answers the research question: what does the current literature report on AI-generated code plagiarism detection in higher education? Presents a systematic literature mapping of current research on detecting AI-generated code plagiarism in academic settings.
inclusion_reason: LLM-generated code detection (educational). Code-specific but about passive plagiarism/detection, not watermarking — useful only as background/context for why provenance of AI-generated code matters in education, not as evidence for our watermarking-method corpus itself.

title: Hiding in Plain Sight: On the Robustness of AI-Generated Code Detection
authors: Saman Pordanesh; Sufiyan Bukhari; Benjamin Tan; Lorenzo De Carli
abstract: AI code assistants, such as GitHub Copilot, are an increasingly popular coding aid, but they also present risks. Large language models (LLMs) upon which those assistants are built may generate insecure/incorrect code, either by accident or as a result of code poisoning attacks. In general, LLMs obfuscate the lineage of source code used for training, which is a problem in contexts such as supply chain security, where tracking provenance is of the utmost importance. While a number of recent approaches can flag AI-generated code based on a combination of lexical and syntactic features, such works have not been evaluated in realistic settings. We identify and operationalize a number of recently proposed AI code identification tools, measuring their baseline performance on datasets generated by state-of-the-art models, then verify the robustness of such approaches to variations in training sets and prompting strategies.
inclusion_reason: LLM-generated code detection (robustness). Code-specific but evaluates passive detection tools, not watermarking — relevant as context/methodological parallel (its robustness-testing protocol against training/prompting variation is a useful model for how we might evaluate watermark robustness), not as a watermarking primary study.

title: AI-Generated Code Detection: An Examination of Current Tools in Education
authors: J. Esteban Cuellar Argotty; R. Manrique
venue: ITS 2025 (Generative Systems and Intelligent Tutoring Systems), Springer Nature Switzerland
abstract: Evaluated seven AI-generated code detection tools across 1,644 code samples and found critical precision-recall trade-offs, with significant performance drops when code was even slightly modified. Concludes that current AI detection tools are unreliable for practical use in educational settings.
inclusion_reason: LLM-generated code detection (educational). Code-specific but about passive detection tools, not watermarking — useful only as background evidence that passive detection is unreliable, reinforcing the case for active watermarking as a proactive alternative (as the review's own Introduction argues), not as a watermarking primary study.

title: Automatic detection of LLM-generated code: A comparative case study of contemporary models across function and class granularities
authors: Musfiqur Rahman; SayedHassan Khatoonabadi; Ahmad Abdellatif; et al.
abstract: The adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) for code generation risks incorporating vulnerable code into software systems. Existing detectors face two critical limitations: a lack of systematic cross-model validation and opaque "black box" operation. We address this through a comparative study of code generated by four distinct LLMs: GPT-3.5, Claude 3 Haiku, Claude Haiku 4.5, and GPT-OSS. Analyzing 14,485 Python functions and 11,913 classes from the CodeSearchNet dataset, we generated corresponding code with all four LLMs. Using interpretable software metrics, we trained CatBoost classifiers for each configuration. Our analysis reveals that granularity effects dominate model differences by a factor of 8.6, with negligible feature overlap, indicating that function-level and class-level detection rely on fundamentally disjoint structural signatures. We discover critical granularity-dependent inversions: while modern models (Claude, GPT-OSS) are more detectable at the class level, GPT-3.5 is an anomaly that uniquely excels at the function level. SHAP analysis identifies the Comment-to-Code Ratio as the sole universal discriminator, though its predictive magnitude varies drastically across models, explaining why detectors trained on specific LLMs fail to generalize. Our findings demonstrate that GPT-3.5's exceptional detectability (AUC-ROC 0.96) is unrepresentative of contemporary models (AUC-ROC approximately between 0.68 and 0.80). Robust detection requires moving beyond single-model studies to account for substantial diversity in structural fingerprints across architectures and granularities.
inclusion_reason: LLM-generated code detection. Code-specific but purely passive/stylometric detection (no watermarking) — relevant as background on why passive detection struggles to generalize across models and granularities (motivating active watermarking), and as a source of resources (CodeSearchNet-derived function/class datasets) potentially reusable for RQ2, but not a watermarking primary study.

title: Watermarking Large Language Models and the Generated Content: Opportunities and Challenges
abstract: The widely adopted and powerful generative large language models (LLMs) have raised concerns about intellectual property rights violations and the spread of machine-generated misinformation. Watermarking serves as a promising approach to establish ownership, prevent unauthorized use, and trace the origins of LLM-generated content. This paper summarizes and shares the challenges and opportunities we found when watermarking LLMs. We begin by introducing techniques for watermarking LLMs themselves under different threat models and scenarios. Next, we investigate watermarking methods designed for the content generated by LLMs, assessing their effectiveness and resilience against various attacks. We also highlight the importance of watermarking domain-specific models and data, such as those used in code generation, chip design, and medical applications. Furthermore, we explore methods like hardware acceleration to improve the efficiency of the watermarking process. Finally, we discuss the limitations of current approaches and outline future research directions for the responsible use and protection of these generative AI tools.
inclusion_reason: LLM text-watermarking survey (background). Partially meets the bar: unlike the other three general surveys, its abstract explicitly names code generation as one of the domain-specific settings it discusses (alongside chip design and medical applications), though code is not its primary focus. Worth a closer read of its code-generation section specifically, but not code-dedicated enough to be a strong snowballing seed on its own.
